title: Foundations: Providence
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Relationship Between Creation and Providence
subpoints: Providence is the twin doctrine to creation, describing God's ongoing interaction with His creation.
These two doctrines cover all of God's actions in the world, distinct from doctrines describing God's intrinsic attributes (like the Trinity or Aseity).
God's sovereignty is the dominant attribute relating to providence, grounded in His omniscience, power, wisdom, and goodness.

outline.title: Confessional Definitions of Providence
subpoints: The Westminster Confession (Ch. 3 & 5) defines God's decrees as wise, holy, and unchangeable acts of His will.
Providence involves God upholding, directing, and governing all creatures and actions for His glory.
The Larger Catechism emphasizes that God preserves and orders all things to His own glory.

outline.title: Biblical Foundations of Divine Control
subpoints: Romans 11:36 affirms that all things are from, through, and to God.
Ephesians 1:11-12 teaches that God works all things according to the counsel of His will.
God's predestinating purpose precedes the foundation of the world, establishing His control over history.

outline.title: The Realms of God's Sovereignty
subpoints: God's sovereignty extends to all realms of existence, not just abstractly but specifically.
God is sovereign over nature, as seen in creation, the flood, and the calming of storms.
God is sovereign over historical events, such as the plagues in Egypt, demonstrating His authority over false gods.

summary:
This lesson, the second in the 'Foundations' series, explores the doctrine of providence as the twin counterpart to the doctrine of creation. While creation describes God's origin of all things, providence addresses His ongoing governance, preservation, and ordering of the universe. The sermon clarifies that while doctrines like the Trinity describe God's intrinsic nature, providence focuses on how God interacts with His creation, particularly moral agents like humans and angels. Central to this doctrine is the attribute of God's sovereignty, which is grounded in His omniscience, power, wisdom, and goodness.

The teaching draws heavily on the Westminster Standards, specifically the Confession of Faith and the Catechisms, to define providence as God's wise and holy act of upholding and directing all creatures and actions for His glory. It emphasizes that God's decrees are unchangeable and that He is not the author of sin, yet He governs all events according to His immutable counsel. The sermon highlights that this theological formulation is not abstract but has practical implications for understanding God's authority over all aspects of life.

Biblical evidence is presented to support these confessional statements, citing Romans 11:36 and Ephesians 1:11-12 to demonstrate that all things proceed from and are governed by God's will. The lesson further illustrates the realms of God's sovereignty by examining His control over nature and history, referencing events such as the creation, the flood, and the plagues in Egypt. These examples serve to affirm that God's authority is comprehensive, extending from the natural world to the specific unfolding of historical events, thereby establishing a robust foundation for trusting in His providential care.
